phonemes.desc: aspirated k (χ), a hard stop released with a strong breath — not the fricative of modern Greek
long close ē (ει), carrying the high pitch of the acute accent
long open ō (ω) with final n

pronunciation.approximation: 'KHEH-rōn' — long ē, long ō, the pitch rising on the first syllable

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: χείρ (kheír), 'hand' — the traditional association of the name, possibly a folk etymology

kin.label: PIE
kin.form: if the link holds, χείρ descends from PIE *ǵʰésr- 'hand' (cf. Hittite keššar); the name's own derivation remains uncertain — Beekes treats the connection cautiously

pronunciation.note: Tier 1: the Greek original Χείρων carries both stress (the acute on ει) and long vowels (ει and ω). The restored form Cheírōn preserves both marks — the accent and the macron — that plain ASCII 'Cheiron' erases.

domains.title: The Most Just of Centaurs
domains.subtitle: Wisdom · Teaching · Heroes
domains.lead: Cheírōn is the exception among the wild κένταυροι: the immortal son of Kronos who dwells in a cave on Mount Pelion and turns raw princes into heroes. Where his kin are drunkards and rapine, Homer calls him δικαιότατος Κενταύρων — the most just of centaurs. He is the teacher: medicine for Asklepios, the lyre and the remedies for Achilles, the whole heroic craft for Iason and Herakles.

cards.name: The Tutor's Craft
cards.desc: He reared Achilles, Iásōn, and Asklepios on Mount Pēlion — 'the most just of the Centaurs' (Iliad 11.832).

cards.name: The Healing Hand
cards.desc: He taught Asklepios the art of drugs, and was himself struck by Herakles' hydra-venomed arrow that no healing art could cure.

cards.name: The Hunter's Art
cards.desc: From him the heroes learned the chase itself — tracking, coursing, and spear-work in the mountain wilds.

cards.name: The Incurable Wound
cards.desc: Herakles' stray arrow, dipped in the Lernaean hydra's venom, struck his knee — the healer whom no remedy could heal (Apollodorus, Library 2.5.4).

symbols.name: The Pelian Ash Spear
symbols.meaning: The great spear of ash wood that Cheírōn cut on Pelion's peak and gave to Peleus at his wedding — the same spear Achilles alone could wield (Iliad 16.143–144). The teacher's gift that arms the hero.

symbols.name: The Cave on Mount Pelion
symbols.meaning: His dwelling and school, the legendary academy of heroes; the gods themselves feasted there at the wedding of Peleus and Thetis (Pindar, Pythian 3.86–95).

symbols.name: The Lyre
symbols.meaning: The instrument of the education he gave Achilles, who in Iliad 9 (186–189) is found in his hut singing the glories of heroes to the lyre.

symbols.name: Herbs and Remedies (φάρμακα)
symbols.meaning: The healing lore he taught Asklepios and gave to Peleus's line; Achilles treats wounds with remedies 'that Cheiron gave his father' (Iliad 4.219, 11.831–832).

symbols.name: The Hydra-Poisoned Arrow
symbols.meaning: Herakles's stray arrow, dipped in the Lernaean hydra's venom, that struck his knee and gave the immortal an unhealable wound (Apollodorus, Library 2.5.4).

symbols.name: The Stars
symbols.meaning: Zeus set him in the sky — remembered as Centaurus or Sagittarius — after he surrendered his immortality and died (Ovid, Fasti 5.379–414; Hyginus, Astronomica 2.38).

mythology.lead: Cheírōn stands at the hinge of two orders: Titan-born yet honored by the Olympians, beast-bodied yet the very image of wisdom. His myths are the myths of transmission — what one generation hands to the next.

myths.title: Son of Kronos and Philyra
myths.text: Kronos lay with the Oceanid Philyra in the shape of a horse, and from that union was born a child of double nature — half god, half horse (Apollodorus, Library 1.2.4). Pindar names him 'the son of Philyra and Kronos', making Cheírōn the half-brother of Zeus and Poseidon (Pythian 4.102–115) — an older generation's blood serving the new order. Philyra, ashamed of her foal, begged to be changed into anything else and became a linden tree, under which the infant was found and reared by Apollo and Artemis; from them he drew the arts he would spend eternity handing on. The myth's double nature runs deeper than the body: the wisest of teachers begins as the child of deception and rejection, and his school in the cave on Pelion is founded by the one centaur whom the gods did not exile from their company.

myths.title: Tutor of the Heroes
myths.text: Pindar gives the roll of his pupils: in his cave Cheírōn reared Iason, gentle-handed Asklepios whom he taught the craft of remedies, and Achilles, whom he fed on the marrow of lions and wild boars to make him fierce (Nemean 3.43–58). Homer twice seals the bond: Achilles treats wounds with remedies 'that Cheiron gave to his father in friendship' (Iliad 4.218–219), and is the man 'whom Cheiron taught, the most just of the centaurs' — dikaiotatos Kentaurōn (Iliad 11.831–832). Actaeon and Herakles also passed through his tutelage. When the Argo sailed, the centaur came down from Pelion to see her off and give the Argonauts his blessing for the voyage (Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica 1.553–558). And in Pindar's grief for the sick Hieron, the poet's deepest wish is that Cheírōn still lived in his cave, that another healer might rise from Pelion and sail to Sicily (Pythian 3.1–7). The school had an address, and the whole Greek world knew it.

myths.title: The Spear for Peleus
myths.text: When Peleus married the sea-goddess Thetis, the gods came down from Olympus and the wedding feast was held on Pelion in Cheírōn's cave; the centaur gave the bridegroom a spear of mountain ash cut from Pelion's peak (Pindar, Pythian 3.86–95; Iliad 16.143–144). That spear passed to Achilles, and at Troy no other Achaean could wield it — Patroklos himself left it behind when he donned Achilles's armor, 'heavy, huge, and strong, which no other of the Achaeans could brandish' (Iliad 16.140–144). The teacher's gift thus runs through the whole Iliad: it is the one weapon that marks the hero his pupil became. The marriage it honored also produced the child Cheírōn would raise — the spear, like the school, was an investment in Achilles before Achilles existed. And when the child was old enough, the centaur received him on Pelion and took up the education the gift had already begun.

myths.title: The Immortal Who Chose Death
myths.text: When Herakles fought the wild centaurs at the cave of Pholos, one of his arrows — tipped with the hydra's incurable venom — struck Cheírōn's knee (Apollodorus, Library 2.5.4). The poison that no healer could answer burned in the flesh of the greatest healer of all; immortal, he could neither heal nor die, and the Iliad preserves the grim acknowledgment — 'Cheiron, the most just of centaurs, whom the gods taught, and whom Herakles's shaft slew' (11.831–832, where even epic grammar staggers at the thought). Sophocles remembers the shaft as the one 'wherewith Cheiron was struck' (Trachiniae 714–716). At last he surrendered his immortality — offered in some tellings in exchange for Prometheus's release — and was allowed to die; Zeus set him among the stars, and Ovid watches the father of heroes' education take his place in the sky (Fasti 5.379–414; Hyginus, Astronomica 2.38). The teacher's last lesson is mortality itself.

lore.syncretism: Rome changed Cheírōn least of all the Greek figures: he keeps his name as Chiron in Latin, too singular to be merged with any Italian power. What Rome absorbed was his catasterism — Latin poets and star-cataloguers fixed him in the sky, debating whether the Centaurus or the Sagittarius was his (Ovid, Fasti 5; Hyginus, Astronomica 2.38). In later tradition he remains the named exception among his kind: Dante makes him chief of the centaurs who guard the violent in Inferno 12 — still 'Chiron, who nursed Achilles,' still teaching, still assigning duties to his infernal pupils. The word 'centaur' traveled into every European language, but Cheírōn travels as himself, the one monster whom civilization quotes.
lore.culturalLegacy: His name lives in the sky: the minor planet 2060 Chiron, discovered in 1977 between Saturn and Uranus, was named for him and gave its class of objects — the centaurs, bodies orbiting among the giant planets — their collective name. Modern astrology adopted him as the emblem of the wounded healer, the one whose incurable hurt becomes the source of healing for others. Ancient herbalists named the plant centaury (κενταύριον) after the centaurs' healing lore. And the old association of his name with χείρ, the hand, echoes — by the word's own root, not by his name's — in 'surgery', from χειρουργία, 'hand-work.'
lore.extendedMeditation: Cheírōn is the Greek answer to a question the centauromachy asks in stone at Olympia and on the Parthenon: can nature be educated? He is a kentauros — the very type of ungoverned appetite — who is instead called most just. That he is Kronos's son and Zeus's half-brother matters: he belongs to the older, Titan order, yet serves the new one by raising its heroes, as if the wild past could be redeemed only by becoming a teacher. His unhealable wound completes the thought — the master of remedies cannot master his own pain, and immortality becomes not a privilege but a sentence. That he must surrender deathlessness to find release is among the most quietly radical moments in Greek myth: even an immortal may long for the human portion.
sources: Sophocles, Trachiniae 714–716; Ovid, Fasti 5.379–414; Hyginus, Astronomica 2.38
Beekes, Etymological Dictionary of Greek, s.v. χείρ
lore.archaeology: No great temple of Cheírōn is known; he is a daimonic tutor, not an Olympian with a state cult, though a cave above Portaria on Mount Pelion is traditionally identified as the Cheironeion, his school. His real monument is the art: Attic black- and red-figure vases repeatedly show Peleus handing the infant Achilles into the centaur's arms, and Roman sarcophagi of the 2nd–3rd c. CE show him teaching the lyre — the 'education of Achilles' among the most copied sarcophagus compositions of the empire. The sculpted centauromachies — the Olympia west pediment and the Parthenon south metopes — preserve the wild centaur type against which his justice was defined.
